Thanks for clarifying. I think I disagree with you. 

When we choose exercise vs eating cakes we are not engaging in the same kind of “drives” based action. 

The attraction to cakes emerges out of a fundamental drive for survival here and now. Body needs easy calories so cakes taste so damn good. 

The “drive” for exercise is a higher order drive. It requires activity from areas of the brain dealing with abstract processing and long term planning. 

The difference is eating the cakes is activated by one drive, exercising is a process of higher cognitive drives regulating the impulse to follow the more basic survival drive.

Even if you don’t like the elephant and rider metaphor you have to agree there are useful destinations to be made in our cognitive processing. 

Daniel Kahniman makes the distinction “thinking fast/ thinking slow”. 

Joshua Greene uses a metaphor of a camera with both an automatic and manual setting. 

Nice little video comparing all three metaphors. 

https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=ShWKLBf5SdA&list=WL&index=2&t=19s


Even Plato used a metaphor of a man and a lion who together could overcome the monster. 

I think they’re useful distinctions to make. One drive to eat cakes vs a network of drives that continuously regulate other drives.

First off you’re conflating logic with rationality. Logic is the process of structuring and ordering inferences. Rationality is the feedback of intelligence on itself to better “ration” resources. 

More important to our seeming impasse. Im not claiming a logical fallacy to your claim that all human action ultimately stems back to some drive. So we do agree about that.

The point I’m trying to make is there are neurological and phenomenological bases for categorizing different drives as having distinct neural and experiential qualities. 

The processing involved in desiring and consuming chocolate cake/ sex/ short term gains are measurably different in nature than long term abstract goals like being healthy/ abstaining from instant gratification. 

In some sense you’re arguing that all matter is the same because its all just atoms interacting with each other. What Im saying is that all may be true on one level, on the human experience level matter manifests itself as very different. 

A chair is very different than a lion even though they’re both just made up of atoms in space.

In the same way it is useful for humans to distinguish between a lion and a chair as fundamentally different objects, it is useful (and empirically tractable) to conceive of our drives as having wholly different qualities.

Im pretty certain that all three are aware of the Homunculus problem, that’s why they never claim there is actually a “rider” or “camera operator” center in the brain. It’s useful only for educational and practical purposes. 

Perhaps you see why being “dangerously close to the Homunculus” is so dangerous in this case, I don’t.
